name: Freedom from fear of the gods and of death
plain_explanation: Epicurus thought most human misery came from fear -- fear that the gods punish us, and fear of what happens after death. He argued both fears rest on false beliefs: the gods, if they exist, are blissfully indifferent to human affairs, and the soul, being made of material atoms, simply disperses at death and can feel nothing afterward, so death is 'nothing to us.'
precise_definition: Epicurus's core therapeutic goal: to remove the two chief sources of human anxiety by philosophical argument -- first, by holding that the gods, though real, do not interfere in or punish human affairs, and second, by holding that the soul is material and dissolves at death, so that the dead have no sensation and therefore cannot suffer.
why_it_mattered: This is presented by Russell as the entire motivating purpose behind Epicurus's otherwise abstract physics: 'It was through the problem of avoiding fear that Epicurus was led into theoretical philosophy.'
historical_origin: Central and original to Epicurus's system from its founding.
examples: 'Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is without sensation, and that which lacks sensation is nothing to us'
Epicurus's view that the gods are rational hedonists who, like his own ideal sage, abstain from the burdens of governing
competing_positions: Popular Greek and 'barbarian' religion, including belief in punishment after death, which Russell says was far more widespread among the general population than surviving elite literature (e.g. depictions on 'Grecian urns') would suggest
influence_on_later_thinkers: Lucretius makes this the emotional center of his poem, treating Epicurus as a liberating hero who defeated the tyranny of Religion.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A direct, sustained philosophical attack on popular religious belief, motivated by its psychological costs rather than by disinterested theology.
